      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Chest</span> Pain</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pain, <span class="qt0">Chest</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Having a pain in your <span class="qt0">chest</span> can be scary.  It does not always mean that you are having a heart attack.  There can be many other causes, including:</p><ul><li>Other heart problems, such as angina</li><li>Panic attacks</li><li>Digestive problems, such as heartburn or esophagus disorders</li><li>Sore muscles</li><li>Lung diseases, such as pneumonia, pleurisy, or pulmonary embolism</li><li>Costochondritis - an inflammation of joints in your <span class="qt0">chest</span></li></ul><p>Some of these problems can be serious.  Get immediate medical care if you have <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain that does not go away, crushing pain or pressure in the <span class="qt0">chest, or chest</span> pain along with nausea, sweating, dizziness or shortness of breath. Treatment depends on the cause of the pain.</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/chestinjuriesanddisorders.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Chest</span> Injuries and Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mediastinal Disorders</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rib Injuries</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Thoracic</span> Injuries</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is the <span class="qt0">chest</span>?<p>The <span class="qt0">chest</span> is the part of your body between your neck and your abdomen (belly). The medical term for your <span class="qt0">chest</span> is <span class="qt1">thorax</span>.</p><p>Your <span class="qt0">chest</span> holds many important structures for breathing, digestion, blood circulation, and other important body functions. These structures include your:</p><ul><li>Ribs and breastbone</li><li>Esophagus, the tube between your mouth and stomach</li><li>Trachea, your windpipe</li><li>Bronchi, the tubes that carry air from your windpipe to your lungs</li><li>Lungs</li><li>Pleura, a thin layer of tissue that covers the lungs and lines the inside wall of the <span class="qt0">chest</span> space</li><li>Heart and large blood vessels</li><li>Thymus, a gland that's part of your immune system</li><li>Nerves</li></ul>What are <span class="qt0">chest</span> injuries and disorders?<p><span class="qt0">Chest</span> injuries and disorders are problems that affect any of the organs or structures located in your <span class="qt0">chest</span>.</p><p>There are many types of <span class="qt0">chest</span> injuries and disorders, for example:</p><ul><li>Broken ribs</li><li>Esophagus disorders</li><li>Swallowing disorders, also called dysphagia</li><li>Tracheal disorders</li><li>Bronchial disorders</li><li>Lung diseases and collapsed lung</li><li>Pleural disorders</li><li>Heart diseases</li><li>Mediastinal diseases, which are tumors, inflammation, and other problems with the structures in the mediastinum, which is the space between your lungs, breastbone, and spine</li><li><span class="qt1">Thoracic</span> aortic aneurysm</li><li><span class="qt1">Thoracic</span> outlet syndrome</li></ul><p><span class="qt0">Chest</span> injuries may happen from the force of car accidents, falls, or sports injuries. Or the <span class="qt0">chest</span> may be pierced by a bullet or sharp object. Because your <span class="qt0">chest</span> holds so many important structures, certain <span class="qt0">chest</span> injuries may be life-threatening.</p>How are <span class="qt0">chest</span> injuries and disorders diagnosed?<p>Diagnosis of <span class="qt0">chest</span> injuries or disorders depends on the type of symptoms you're having and whether you've had a <span class="qt0">chest</span> injury. Injuries are usually obvious, but in most cases, you'll need tests to know how serious an injury is.</p><p>There are many types of tests for diagnosing different types of <span class="qt0">chest</span> injuries and disorders, for example:</p><ul><li>Diagnostic imaging tests</li><li>Heart tests</li><li>Lung function tests</li><li>Bronchoscopy</li><li>Pleural fluid analysis</li><li>Dysphagia tests</li><li>Biopsy</li></ul><p>Treatments will depend on the type of <span class="qt0">chest</span> injury or disorder you have.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/acutebronchitis.html">
      <content name="title">Acute Bronchitis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bronchitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Chest</span> Cold</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes, the airways that carry air to your lungs. It causes a cough that often brings up mucus. It can also cause shortness of breath, wheezing, a low fever, and <span class="qt0">chest</span> tightness. There are two main types of bronchitis: acute and chronic.</p><p>Most cases of acute bronchitis get better within several days. But your cough can last for several weeks after the infection is gone.</p><p>The same viruses that cause colds and the flu often cause acute bronchitis. These viruses spread through the air when people cough, or through physical contact (for example, on unwashed hands). Being exposed to tobacco smoke, air pollution, dust, vapors, and fumes can also cause acute bronchitis. Less often, bacteria can also cause acute bronchitis.</p><p>To diagnose acute bronchitis, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and listen to your breathing. You may also have other tests.</p><p>Treatments include rest, fluids, and aspirin (for adults) or acetaminophen to treat fever. A humidifier or steam can also help. You may need inhaled medicine to open your airways if you are wheezing. Antibiotics won't help if the cause is viral. You may get antibiotics if the cause is bacterial.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/pulmonaryrehabilitation.html">
      <content name="title">Pulmonary Rehabilitation</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Chest</span> Physical Therapy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Lung Rehabilitation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is pulmonary rehabilitation?<p>Pulmonary rehabilitation, also known as pulmonary rehab or PR, is a program for people who have chronic (ongoing) breathing problems. It can help improve your ability to function and quality of life. PR does not replace your medical treatment. Instead, you use them together.</p><p>PR is often an outpatient program that you do in a hospital or clinic. Some people have PR in their homes. You work with a team of health care providers to find ways to lessen your symptoms, increase your ability to exercise, and make it easier to do your daily activities.</p>Who needs pulmonary rehabilitation?<p>Your health care provider may recommend pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) if you have a chronic lung disease or another condition that makes it hard for you to breathe and limits your activities. For example, PR may help you if you:</p><ul><li>Have COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). The two main types are emphysema and chronic bronchitis. In COPD, your airways (tubes that carry air in and out of your lungs) are partially blocked. This makes it hard to get air in and out.</li><li>Have an interstitial lung disease such as sarcoidosis and pulmonary fibrosis. These diseases cause scarring of the lungs over time. This makes it hard to get enough oxygen.</li><li>Have cystic fibrosis (CF). CF is an inherited disease that causes thick, sticky mucus to collect in the lungs and block the airways.</li><li>Need lung surgery. You may have PR before and after lung surgery to help you prepare for and recover from the surgery.</li><li>Have a muscle-wasting disorder that affects the muscles used for breathing. An example is muscular dystrophy.</li></ul><p>PR works best if you start it before your disease is severe. However, even people who have advanced lung disease can benefit from PR.</p>What does pulmonary rehabilitation include?<p>When you first start pulmonary rehabilitation (PR), your team of health care providers will want to learn more about your health. You will have lung function, exercise, and possibly blood tests. Your team will go over your medical history and current treatments. They may check on your mental health and ask about your diet. Then they will work together to create a plan that is right for you. It may include:</p><ul><li>Exercise training. Your team will come up with an exercise plan to improve your endurance and muscle strength. You will likely have exercises for both your arms and legs. You might use a treadmill, stationary bike, or weights. You may need to start slowly and increase your exercise as you get stronger.</li><li>Nutritional counseling. Being either overweight or underweight can affect your breathing. A nutritious eating plan can help you work towards a healthy weight.</li><li>Education about your disease and how to manage it. This includes learning how to avoid situations that make your symptoms worse, how to avoid infections, and how/when to take your medicines.</li><li>Techniques you can use to save your energy. Your team may teach you easier ways to do daily tasks. For example, you may learn ways to avoid reaching, lifting, or bending. Those movements make it harder to breathe, since they use up energy and make you tighten your abdominal muscles. You may also learn how to better deal with stress, since stress can also take up energy and affect your breathing.</li><li>Breathing strategies. You will learn techniques to improve your breathing. These techniques may increase your oxygen levels, decrease how often you take breaths, and keep your airways open longer.</li><li>Psychological counseling and/or group support. It can feel scary to have trouble breathing. If you have a chronic lung disease, you are more likely to have depression, anxiety, or other emotional problems. Many PR programs include counseling and/or support groups. If not, your PR team may be able to refer you to an organization that offers them.</li>
</ul><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/heartdiseaseinwomen.html">
      <content name="title">Heart Disease in Women</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is heart disease?<p>Heart disease is a general term that includes many types of heart problems. It's also called cardiovascular disease, which means heart and blood vessel disease.</p><p>Coronary artery disease (also called coronary heart disease) is the most common type of heart disease in both men and women. It happens slowly over time when a sticky substance called plaque builds up in the arteries that supply your heart muscle with blood. The plaque narrows or blocks blood flow to the heart muscle and can lead to:</p><ul><li>Angina - <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain from lack of blood flow</li><li>Heart attacks - when part of the heart muscle dies from loss of blood flow</li><li>Heart failure - when your heart can't pump enough blood to meet your body's needs</li><li>Arrhythmia - a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat</li></ul>How does heart disease affect women?<p>In the United States, heart disease is the number one cause of death in women. But women are often not diagnosed with heart disease as quickly as men are. That's because:</p><ul><li>Women are more likely than men to have "silent" heart disease, meaning that they don't have symptoms.</li><li>Health care providers may not recognize heart disease in women because women's symptoms may be different from men's symptoms.</li><li>Women are more likely than men to have certain types of heart disease that can be harder to diagnose.</li></ul><p>A delay in diagnosis may mean a delay in medical care that could help prevent serious problems, such as a heart attack. That's why it's important to learn about your risk for heart disease, the symptoms in women, and how to keep your heart healthy.</p>What types of heart disease do women get?<p>Women can get any type of heart disease. Like men, the most common type of heart disease among women is coronary artery disease. But there are certain types of heart disease which are less common, but affect women more often than men:</p><ul><li>Coronary microvascular disease - <span class="qt0">Chest</span> pain from spasms (sudden tightening) in the smallest arteries of the heart that pinch off blood flow. It typically happens during rest or routine activities. This serious condition increases your risk of having a heart attack or other heart diseases.  This type may be harder to diagnose since blockages in smaller arteries can be harder to see on imaging tests.</li><li>Broken heart syndrome - Strong <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain or other signs that look like a heart attack. It's caused by the stress of powerful emotions, such as deep grief, anger, or surprise. It can happen even if you're healthy. It mostly affects women after menopause and usually doesn't cause any lasting damage.</li><li>Variant angina - A rare type of strong <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain from spasms in the heart arteries. The pain usually happens in a pattern during sleep. Variant angina rarely causes a heart attack.</li></ul>Which women are more likely to develop heart disease?<p>Your risk for developing heart disease increases with:</p><ul><li>Menopause. Women can develop heart disease at any age, but your risk increases after your periods stop, usually by age 55. Before menopause, your body makes more estrogen (a female hormone) which helps protect against heart disease. That's why women generally develop coronary artery disease 10 years later than men. During and after menopause, estrogen levels drop and your risk for heart diseases goes up. If your periods stop before age 40, your risk will be higher than other women your age.</li><li>Family history of heart disease. Your risk for heart disease may be higher if your:
	<ul><li>Mother or sister had heart disease before age 65.</li><li>Father or brother had heart disease before age 55.</li></ul>
</li><li>Problems during pregnancy, such as  high blood pressure, gestational diabetes, anemia, and high blood pressure.</li><li>Use of hormonal birth control (pills, patches, or vaginal rings with estrogen and progesterone).</li><li>Endometriosis.</li><li>Polycystic ovary syndrome.</li><li>Inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.</li><li>Metabolic syndrome.</li><li>Mental health issues, such as stress, anxiety, or depression.</li><li>Health risks from a lack physical activity.</li><li>Obesity or being overweight.</li><li>Diabetes.</li><li>Low HDL cholesterol levels.</li><li>Mild to moderate high blood pressure.</li><li>Smoking.</li></ul><p>If you have one or more risks for heart disease, ask your health care provider for help understanding your risk level. Ask if you need any heart tests to help catch heart disease early.</p>What are the symptoms of heart disease and heart attack in women?<p>When women have symptoms of heart disease, they may include:</p><ul><li>Pain or discomfort in the <span class="qt0">chest</span> that may be dull and heavy or sharp</li><li>Pain in the neck, jaw, throat, upper belly, or back</li><li>Nausea or vomiting</li><li>Unusual fatigue</li><li>Shortness of breath (feeling like you can't get enough air) during physical activity</li></ul><p>Women who have coronary artery disease are more likely than men to have <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain when resting or doing daily activities, rather than during exercise. They're also more likely than men to feel <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain from mental stress.</p><p>Symptoms of a heart attack in women may also be different than in men. <span class="qt0">Chest</span> pain is the most common symptom for both sexes. It may feel like crushing or squeezing. But women are somewhat less likely than men to have <span class="qt0">chest</span> pain.</p><p>During a heart attack, women may feel:</p><ul><li>Pressure or tightness in the <span class="qt0">chest</span></li><li>Pain in the upper back, arms, neck, jaw or throat</li><li>Dizziness</li><li>Unusual fatigue</li><li>Indigestion, heartburn, nausea, or vomiting </li><li>Stomach pain</li><li>Shortness of breath</li></ul><p>Heart attacks usually don't look like the sudden, dramatic events we see in the movies. The symptoms may be mild or strong. They may start slowly. They can stop and then come back.</p>Can heart disease in women be prevented?<p>You can help lower your risk by:</p><ul><li>Learning how to prevent heart disease and making heart-healthy habits part of your daily life.</li><li>Asking your provider about your personal risk for heart disease and the best way to manage your heart health.</li></ul><p>Remember, women can have heart disease without symptoms. But if you pay attention to your risk for heart disease, you can take action to prevent problems or keep them from getting worse.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>
